title: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because useful variations appear only occasionally, keeping a large number of individuals greatly increases the chance of useful variations appearing and is of the highest importance to success in selection.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But as variations manifestly useful or pleasing to man appear only occasionally, the chance of their appearance will be much increased by a large number of individuals being kept; and hence this comes to be of the highest importance to success.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Circumstances favourable to Man’s power of Selection”. Scope: artificial selection on domesticated animals and plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-16: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The sampling prediction follows directly from rare-variant probability and is testable in many archived breeding and experimental datasets. Full taxonomic scope is unnecessary to discriminate the stated mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate the probability of observing beneficial variants as a function of census or screened population size while controlling mutation rate and selection protocol. A rising discovery probability and stronger selection response with larger samples supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Useful variants are context dependent.

Breeding programs differ in effort and genetic diversity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.92
analysis feasibility: 0.79
data adequacy: 0.51
discriminating power: 0.85
data existence: 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Population-size catalogues and variant archives proxy the sampling half of the statement for a few domestic species. They do not record the appearance of variations that breeders find useful, which is the outcome that would have to be compared with other ingredients of success. The testable residue is a confounded correlation between herd size and gain, not a clean ranking of causes.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate the rate at which useful or selected variants appear, or the rate of genetic gain, to the number of individuals kept, holding heritability and generation interval fixed. A strong positive partial association would support the importance of numbers; no association once effort and heritability are controlled would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Breeding-programme gain, census size, and investment are rarely public in the same table and are strongly confounded.

Once useful variants are assumed to be rare and random, a larger herd raising the chance they appear is close to a sampling identity.

Sequencing depth is not the same variable as the number of animals a breeder keeps.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.42
analysis feasibility: 0.38
data existence: 0.4
operationalizability: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.3
